etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Inherited from Middle English sclave, from Old French sclave, from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”), traditionally assumed to be because Slavs were often forced into slavery in the Middle Ages. The Latin word is from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos); see that entry and Slav for more. Displaced native Old English þēow. Thrall and bondsman/bondswoman, however, remain common synonyms. Doublet of ciao and Slav.

An alternative hypothesis derives sclavus from Ancient Greek σκῡλεύω (skūleúō), σκῡλάω (skūláō, “to strip or despoil a slain enemy”).

definitions.definition: A person who is held in servitude as the property of another person, and whose labor (and often also whose body and life) is subject to the owner's volition and control.

quote.citation: 1963, C.L.R. James, The Black Jacobins, 2nd Revised edition, page 9:
quote.text: Fear of their cargo bred a savage cruelty into the crew. One captain, to strike terror into the rest, killed a slave and dividing heart, liver and entrails into 300 pieces made each of the slaves eat one, threatening those who refused with the same torture. Such incidents were not rare.

definitions.definition: (figuratively) A drudge; one who labors or is obliged (e.g. by prior contract) to labor like a slave with limited rights, e.g. an indentured servant.

quote.citation: 1598–1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, Much Adoe about Nothing. […], quarto edition, London:  […]  V[alentine] S[immes] for Andrew Wise, and William Aspley, published 1600, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: Art thou the ſlaue that with thy breath haſt kill'd / Mine innocent child?

definitions.definition: (figuratively) One who has no power of resistance to something, one who surrenders to or is under the domination of something.

quote.citation: 1985, “Slave to the Rhythm”, in Slave to the Rhythm, performed by Grace Jones:
quote.text: Slave to the rhythm! / Keep it up, keep it up! / Never stop! Never stop!

definitions.definition: (BDSM) A submissive partner in a BDSM relationship who consensually submits to, sexually or personally, serving one or more masters or mistresses.

quote.citation: [2016, Ariane Cruz, The Color of Kink: Black Women, BDSM, and Pornography, NYU Press, →ISBN, page 39:
quote.text: In the clip the black female “slave” dons a chain around her neck for which her white mistress possesses the key. The black woman sub is further disciplined by the power of speech—the force of silence.]

definitions.definition: A sex slave, a person who is forced against their will to perform, for another person or group, sexual acts on a regular or continuing basis.
(engineering, computing, photography) A device (such as a secondary flash or hard drive) that is subject to the control of another (a master).

quote.citation: 2011, Roderick W. Smith, LPIC-2 Linux Professional Institute Certification Study Guide, John Wiley & Sons, →ISBN:
quote.text: If you administer your own reverse DNS zones, remember to include them in your slave configuration.

definitions.definition: To work as a slaver, to enslave people.

quote.citation: 1606, John Marston, The Wonder of Women:
quote.text: MASSINISSA: Wilt thou be slaved? SOPHONISBA: No, free

quote.citation: 1908, James Wells, Stewart of Lovedale: The Life of James Stewart, D.D., M.D., Hon. F.R.G.S., page 88:
quote.text: The truth is from the Zambesi to Lake Nyasa on the north and east banks of the  river, there is nothing but slaving — Africans selling each other . . .

quote.citation: 2011, David Eltis, Keith Bradley, Paul Cartledge, The Cambridge World History of Slavery: Volume 3, AD 1420-AD 1804, Cambridge University Press, →ISBN, page 128:
quote.text: Despite these examples, the majority of enslaved Africans were not able to rely on rulers for help against slaving. Africans living in chiefdoms and villages ruled by allied African authorities were, however, able to use the legal system (Tribunal of Mukanos) in place in the regions under formal Portuguese control  […]

quote.citation: 2016, Thomas Arcaro, Rosemary Haskell, Chinedu Eke, Robert Anderson, Stephen Braye, Ann Cahill, Brian Digre, Anne Bolin, Mathew Gendle, Duane McClearn, Jeffrey Pugh, Laura Roselle, Jean Schwind, Kerstin Sorensen, Anthony Weston, Understanding the Global Experience: Becoming a Responsible World Citizen, Routledge, →ISBN:
quote.text: With ready access to firearms through trade, the slaving Africans held a distinct upper-hand over the groups they preyed upon, which were often politically and socially weakened or destroyed by the trade.

quote.citation: 2016, Alistair Paterson, A Millennium of Cultural Contact, Routledge, →ISBN, page 117:
quote.text: Significant impacts resulted from slaving; there is evidence of how communities dealt with the threat and benefits of slaving. Africans provided most of the slaves to European slavers. Most slaves were created either to settle debts or raise funds, through warfare, or as punishment for a real or perceived crime.
